1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. ML: machine learning; RDS: Relational Database Service; EMR: Elastic MapReduce; CTAS: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT; ANSI: American National Standards Institute; EC2: Elastic Compute Cloud; MSK: Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka; BI: business intelligence; RLS: row-level security

  • Visualize data with Amazon QuickSight (Amazon Quick), DataBrew and other tools
  • Verify and clean data with Lambda, Athena, QuickSight, Jupyter notebooks and SageMaker Data Wrangler
  • Use SQL in Amazon Redshift and Athena to query data and create views
  • Explore data with Athena notebooks that use Apache Spark
  • Describe the trade-offs between provisioned and serverless services
  • Define aggregation, rolling average, grouping and pivoting

2Visualizing Data (skill 3.2.1)

Running case

Kestrel Freight Builds Dashboards

  • Operations wants a live on-time-delivery dashboard
  • Finance wants monthly cost by route, refreshed each morning
  • Engineers want pipeline health on a time-series chart
  • Your job: pick the visualization tool and the data path for each
Tool Best for Remember
Amazon QuickSight (now part of Amazon Quick) Old name Business intelligence dashboards, ad hoc analysis, embedded analytics, ML insights Serverless; SPICE (Super-fast, Parallel, In-memory Calculation Engine) for fast imported data or direct query; sources Athena (S3), Redshift, RDS, Aurora, OpenSearch and many more; row-level security; pay per user or session
AWS Glue DataBrew Visual profiling of a dataset (distributions, missing values, correlations) For preparation, not dashboards
Amazon Managed Grafana Operational and time-series dashboards Managed Grafana for CloudWatch, Prometheus, OpenSearch, Timestream and more
OpenSearch Dashboards Log and event exploration Included with Amazon OpenSearch Service
Jupyter notebooks (SageMaker, EMR Studio, Athena) Exploratory analysis in code Python, SQL, charts
  • QuickSight data path: datasets (from a source or SQL query) → SPICE import (fast, scheduled refresh, up to the capacity) or direct query (always current, slower, loads the source) → analyses → dashboards shared with readers
  • Athena as a source lets QuickSight chart S3 data lakes through the Glue Data Catalog
Exam tip

"Interactive dashboards on S3 data, no servers" → QuickSight with Athena. "Time-series operational metrics" → Managed Grafana.

3Verifying and Cleaning Data (skill 3.2.2)

Tool How it verifies or cleans
AWS Lambda Small, event-driven checks on arriving files or records (schema, ranges, formats); reject or fix
Amazon Athena SQL checks over S3 data: counts, nulls, duplicates, outliers, referential checks; CTAS to write a clean copy
Amazon QuickSight Charts and filters reveal gaps, spikes and odd categories
Jupyter notebooks Python (pandas, PySpark) for exploratory cleaning
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler Visual data preparation for ML and analytics inside SageMaker (profiles, hundreds of built-in transforms, quality insights)
AWS Glue DataBrew Profile and clean visually (Module 10)
  • Common cleaning tasks: remove duplicates, handle nulls (drop, fill, flag), fix types and formats, standardize units, case and time zones, trim and parse text, validate against rules, detect and treat outliers
  • Verify with row counts before and after, checksums, sample comparisons and data quality rules (Module 13)

4SQL in Amazon Redshift and Athena (skill 3.2.3)

  • Both use ANSI-style SQL: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, subqueries and CTEs (WITH), window functions, set operations
  • Views: a view saves a query. Athena views are logical (stored in the Glue Data Catalog, run each time). Redshift views are logical, with late-binding views that do not depend on the underlying objects at creation (needed for Spectrum external tables); materialized views store results (Module 6)
  • Athena SQL runs on S3 data (Trino and Presto based); Redshift SQL runs on warehouse tables and Spectrum external tables (PostgreSQL based)
  • Use views for: reusable logic, hiding columns or rows, stable names over changing tables, simplifying joins for analysts
  • Performance habits: select only needed columns, filter on partition and sort keys, join on distribution keys, avoid SELECT * on wide columnar data
-- A reusable view of late shipments
CREATE VIEW late_shipments AS
SELECT s.shipment_id, c.name AS customer, s.promised_date, s.delivered_date
FROM   shipments s JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHERE  s.delivered_date > s.promised_date;

5Aggregation, Grouping, Rolling Averages and Pivoting (skill 3.2.6)

  • Aggregation: combine many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
  • Grouping: GROUP BY makes one result row per group (per route, per month); HAVING filters groups after aggregation, WHERE filters rows before
  • Window function: calculates across related rows without collapsing them: OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)
  • Rolling (moving) average: an average over a sliding window, such as the last 7 days, to smooth noise and show trends
SELECT day,
       AVG(delay_minutes) OVER (ORDER BY day
            ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rolling_7_day_delay
FROM   daily_delays;
  • Pivoting: turn row values into columns (months across the top) for reports; in Redshift use PIVOT, in Athena use conditional aggregation (SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Jan' THEN cost END)); unpivot does the reverse
  • Related ideas: running total (SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY ...)), rank (RANK, ROW_NUMBER), percentiles, cube and rollup subtotals
Exam tip

"Smooth daily values with the average of the last 7 days" → a window function with a rolling frame. "Show months as columns" → pivot.

6Athena Notebooks with Apache Spark (skill 3.2.4)

  • Amazon Athena for Apache Spark runs interactive Spark without clusters: you work in notebooks (in the Athena console or SageMaker Unified Studio) with sessions that start in seconds
  • Write PySpark or Spark SQL to explore, join, reshape and chart data in S3, using the Glue Data Catalog; no infrastructure to manage, pay for compute while the session runs
  • Use it when: SQL alone is not enough (custom Python, machine-learning-style prep, complex reshaping) but you do not want an EMR cluster
  • Compare: Athena SQL = simple, per-data-scanned; Athena Spark = code and exploration, serverless; EMR / Glue = production pipelines at scale
Exam tip

"Explore S3 data with PySpark in a notebook and no cluster to manage" → Athena notebooks with Apache Spark.

7Provisioned versus Serverless (skill 3.2.5)

Provisioned Serverless
Capacity You choose size and count Automatic scaling
Cost shape Pay while it exists (reserved or committed discounts possible) Pay for use; nothing when idle
Best for Steady, predictable, heavy workloads Spiky, unpredictable, occasional or new workloads
Control Tuning, versions, instance types Less control
Drawbacks Over- or under-provisioning, operations Startup or cold-start time, limits and quotas, can cost more at constant high use
Need Provisioned option Serverless option
Data warehouse Redshift provisioned (RA3) Redshift Serverless
Big data processing EMR on EC2 EMR Serverless, AWS Glue
SQL on S3 Redshift Spectrum on a cluster Athena
Streaming Kinesis provisioned shards, MSK Provisioned Kinesis on-demand, MSK Serverless
Relational RDS, Aurora provisioned Aurora Serverless v2
Key-value DynamoDB provisioned DynamoDB on-demand
Search OpenSearch Service domains OpenSearch Serverless
Exam tip

"Unpredictable or spiky analytics, pay only when queries run" → Redshift Serverless or Athena. "Constant heavy workload with predictable cost" → provisioned with reserved capacity.

8Exam Q&A

8.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Operations at Kestrel Freight want interactive dashboards on data in an S3 data lake, shared with many readers, with no servers to manage. Which combination fits best?

  • AAmazon EMR with a custom web application for the charts
  • BAmazon QuickSight with Amazon Athena as the data source
  • CAmazon Kinesis Data Streams feeding a dashboard directly
  • DAWS Glue crawlers that draw charts from the tables
Show the answer

Answer: B. QuickSight is a serverless BI service, and Athena exposes S3 data through the Glue Data Catalog.

S2An analyst needs the average delivery delay for the last 7 days, calculated for each day, to smooth daily noise. Which SQL approach is correct?

  • AGROUP BY day with the AVG function applied to each day alone
  • BSELECT DISTINCT on the day and delay columns of the table
  • CA CROSS JOIN of the table with a calendar table of days
  • DA window function AVG(...) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
Show the answer

Answer: D. A window function with a rolling frame computes a moving average without collapsing rows.

S3A report must show months as columns with total cost per route in the rows, using Athena. Which technique should be used?

  • AA UNION of the monthly tables, one table after another
  • BConditional aggregation such as SUM(CASE WHEN month = 'Jan' THEN cost END) by route
  • CAn INNER JOIN of the cost table to itself on the month column
  • DAn ORDER BY month clause with a LIMIT on the result
Show the answer

Answer: B. Pivoting turns row values into columns; Athena does this with conditional aggregation.

S4A data scientist wants to explore data in S3 with PySpark in a notebook without managing a cluster. Which service feature fits?

  • AAmazon EMR on EC2 with a long-running cluster
  • BAWS Backup
  • CAmazon Athena notebooks with Apache Spark
  • DAmazon MQ
Show the answer

Answer: C. Athena for Apache Spark provides serverless interactive Spark sessions in notebooks over data in S3.

S5A company has unpredictable, occasional heavy analytics and does not want to pay for idle capacity. Which TWO options match? (Select TWO.)

  • AA fixed fleet of EMR on EC2 nodes
  • BA provisioned Kinesis stream sized for peak
  • CA large Redshift RA3 cluster running 24 hours a day
  • DAmazon Redshift Serverless
  • EAmazon Athena
Show the answer

Answer: D, E. Both are serverless and charge for use, so there is no idle cost. The other options keep paying for capacity.

S6A team wants reusable query logic that hides columns from analysts and gives stable names over changing tables in Athena. What should they create?

  • AA view
  • BA larger workgroup
  • CA new S3 bucket
  • DA crawler
Show the answer

Answer: A. A view stores a query as a reusable logical table, can expose only selected columns and gives a stable name.

9Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Visualization QuickSight (Amazon Quick): serverless BI, SPICE or direct query, Athena/Redshift sources, RLS; Managed Grafana for operational metrics; OpenSearch Dashboards for logs
Cleaning Lambda (small, event), Athena SQL (set-based checks, CTAS), DataBrew / Data Wrangler (visual), notebooks (code), QuickSight (spot outliers)
SQL Views (logical; Redshift late-binding for Spectrum), materialized views store results; select columns, filter keys
Aggregation GROUP BY (rows → groups), HAVING (filter groups), windows (OVER), rolling average (ROWS BETWEEN n PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), pivot (Redshift PIVOT; Athena CASE)
Athena Spark Serverless notebooks, PySpark/Spark SQL, no cluster, pay while the session runs
Provisioned vs serverless Provisioned: steady, control, idle cost. Serverless: spiky, no planning, pay for use, startup and limits; examples Redshift Serverless, EMR Serverless, Aurora Serverless v2, Kinesis on-demand, DynamoDB on-demand, MSK Serverless
